mainTopic: Three views of what the משנה's "הצד השוה שבהן" comes to include
overview: The גמרא first finishes explaining an extra phrase about אש: it includes fire that scorched a plowed field or singed stones without burning them up. Then it asks what the משנה's closing phrase, הצד השוה שבהן (the common feature among them), comes to add. אביי says it adds objects that a normal wind blew off a roof. The גמרא rules out other ways of picturing this case, since they would already be אש or בור. It settles on objects that landed and were made הפקר: they are unlike בור because the wind moved them, so they are learned from what בור and אש share. רבא says the phrase adds an obstacle kicked to a new spot by people or animals. Since the owner did not put it there himself, it is learned from what בור and שור share. רב אדא בר אהבה says it adds gutters and caves emptied into the street with permission. The waste is unlike בור, which is dug without permission, yet the owner still pays if it causes damage.

steps.title: Fire damage that leaves the object intact
steps.stepSummary: The extra phrase about אש comes to include cases where the fire scorched a plowed field or singed stones.
steps.simpleTranslation: It comes to include a case where the fire scorched his plowed field and singed his stones.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its earlier question about what an extra phrase about אש comes to include. It adds fire damage that harms something without burning it up.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A plowed field or stones are not consumed by fire. They are only damaged: the field loses its plowing and the stones crack or are spoiled. The point is that the owner of the fire still pays even though nothing was destroyed.

keyTerms.meaning: To include, to bring in an extra case
It licked or scorched
His plowed field
It singed or damaged

steps.whatToRemember: With אש you are liable even if the fire only damaged something and did not burn it up.

phrases.english: To include where it scorched his plowed field
phrases.notes: "It" is the fire. It burned off the plowed surface, so the field has to be plowed again.

phrases.english: and singed his stones.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question raised just before this passage about what an extra phrase concerning אש adds.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The phrase includes fire damage that harms without consuming: a scorched plowed field and singed stones.

steps.title: What does "the common feature" add?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's phrase "הצד השוה שבהן" and asks what extra case it comes to include.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: "The common feature among them." What does this come to include?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new phrase in the משנה and asks what it adds. This sets up אביי's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא assumes that every phrase in the משנה teaches something. Since the four main damagers were already listed, the general phrase "the common feature" must be there to bring in some damager that was not named.

keyTerms.meaning: The common feature, the shared trait
That is in them, among them
What?

phrases.english: "The common feature among them."
To include what?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the phrase about אש to the משנה's closing general phrase.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which case not already covered by the named damagers is added by "הצד השוה שבהן"?

steps.title: אביי: objects blown off a roof
steps.stepSummary: אביי says the phrase includes a stone, knife, or load left on a roof that fell in a normal wind and caused damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: it comes to include his stone, his knife, or his load that he left on top of his roof, and they fell in a normal wind and caused damage.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי gives the answer: the general phrase adds a case of things left on a roof that a normal wind knocked down, where they then caused damage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These objects are not an animal, a pit, or a fire, yet the owner should still pay. The "common feature" principle brings them in because they share the key traits of the named damagers. The wind is a "normal" one, so the owner should have expected it.

keyTerms.meaning: His load or burden
His roof
A normal, common wind

phrases.english: Abaye said: to include
his stone, his knife, or his load
that he placed on top of his roof,
and they fell in a normal wind and caused damage.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: לְאֵתוֹיֵי אַבְנוֹ סַכִּינוֹ וּמַשָּׂאוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 2.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: "הצד השוה" adds objects left on a roof that fell in a normal wind and caused damage.

steps.title: If they damage while falling, that is just אש
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what exactly אביי's case is. If the objects did damage while being carried by the wind, that is already the category of אש.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If they cause damage while they are moving, that is the same as אש!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges אביי. If the damage happened while the objects were still flying, the case already fits under אש, so the משנה would not need a special phrase for it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question "היכי דמי" asks for the exact case, and the first option is knocked down right away. Fire also does damage while the wind carries it, so falling objects look like a kind of אש. That would make "הצד השוה" unnecessary for this case.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? How do we picture it?
While they are moving
That is the same as
Fire, one of the four main damagers

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not saying אביי is wrong yet. It is only showing that one way of picturing his case adds nothing new.

phrases.english: What are the circumstances?

phrases.aramaic: אִי בַּהֲדֵי דְּקָא אָזְלִי קָא מַזְּקִי –
phrases.english: If they cause damage while they are moving,
that is Fire!

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵיכִי דָּמֵי? אִי בַּהֲדֵי דְּקָא אָזְלִי קָא מַזְּקִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges אביי's answer by trying to pin down his case.
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's claim that "הצד השוה" is needed to include objects blown off a roof.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the objects damage while flying, they are already covered by אש, so no extra phrase is needed.

steps.title: Why falling objects fit the definition of אש
steps.stepSummary: What defines אש is that an outside force helps it do damage and it is your property that you must guard. Both are true of the objects on the roof.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is special about אש? Another force is mixed in with it, and it is your property and you must guard it. These too have another force mixed in with them, and they are your property and you must guard them!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up its challenge by showing that the objects blown off the roof have both features that define אש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Fire has two features: the wind (an outside force) helps spread it, and it belongs to you, so you must guard it. A stone carried by the wind has the same two features. So the case is already part of אש, and אביי's case still needs another explanation.

keyTerms.meaning: What is different? What makes it special?
Another force is mixed in with it
Guarding it is your responsibility
These too

steps.whatToRemember: אש is defined by two features: an outside force helps it do damage, and it is your property that you must guard. Anything with both features already counts as אש.
steps.whyThisMatters: This two-part definition of אש is the measuring stick the גמרא uses to decide what belongs under fire and what needs another source.

phrases.english: What is different about Fire?
That another force is involved with it,
phrases.notes: The "other force" is the wind that carries the fire.

phrases.english: and it is your property and its safeguarding is upon you;

phrases.aramaic: הָנֵי נָמֵי, כֹּחַ אַחֵר מְעוֹרָב בָּהֶן,
phrases.english: these too have another force involved with them,
and they are your property and their safeguarding is upon you!

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי שְׁנָא אֵשׁ – דְּכֹחַ אַחֵר מְעוֹרָב בּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains and supports the claim in step 4 that the falling objects are just אש.
steps.raayaObject: That objects carried by the wind and causing damage in flight fall under אש.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The two defining features of אש: an outside force is involved, and it is your property that you must guard.

steps.title: Maybe the case is after the objects landed, but then it is just בור
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests אביי's case is where the objects did damage after they landed. It challenges this: if the owner made them הפקר, both רב and שמואל agree that this is simply בור.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, maybe the case is after the objects came to rest on the ground. But if he declared them ownerless, then according to both רב and שמואל, that is just בור!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries a second way to read אביי's case: the objects damaged after they were already lying on the ground. It immediately pushes back that this would just be בור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An object lying on the ground that someone trips over works like a pit, because it is a hazard in the street. When the owner gave up ownership by making it הפקר, both רב and שמואל agree it falls under בור. So the משנה would not need הצד השוה to teach it.

keyTerms.meaning: After they come to rest (on the ground)
He declared them ownerless (הֶפְקֵר)
Pit: one of the main categories of damage, a hazard left in the public area

phrases.english: Rather, after they came to rest.
If he declared them ownerless –
both according to Rav and according to Shmuel,
that is the same as Pit!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After rejecting the 'damaged while flying' reading as just אש, the גמרא tries a new reading of אביי's case and attacks it too.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading of אביי's case as damage done after the objects landed and were made הפקר.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Such a case is already covered by בור according to everyone, so הצד השוה would add nothing.

steps.title: Why landed objects fit the definition of בור
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains why these objects are just בור: what makes בור special is that it was made in a way that can cause damage and it is your property to guard. Both are true of these objects.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is special about בור? That from the start it was made in a way that causes damage, and it is your property and you must guard it. These objects too: from the start they were set up in a way that causes damage, and they are your property and you must guard them!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up its challenge by spelling out the defining features of בור. It shows that the objects on the ground share every one of them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Just like step 5 compared the objects to אש, this step compares them to בור. A pit is a hazard from the moment it is dug, and the one responsible must guard it. Objects lying in the street are the same, so they fit right into בור.

keyTerms.meaning: What is different / special about
Its very beginning is set up for damage
Your property
Guarding them is your responsibility

phrases.english: What is special about Pit –
that from its very making it is set up to cause damage,
and it is your property and guarding it is on you;
these too: from their very making they are set up to cause damage,
and they are your property and guarding them is on you!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reasoning behind step 6's claim that the landed objects are simply בור.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that landed, ownerless objects belong under בור.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The defining features of בור: made in a way that damages, and the owner's job to guard it.

steps.title: Maybe he did not make them ownerless, but for שמואל it is still בור
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tries the case where the owner did not make the objects הפקר. It answers that according to שמואל, who learns all obstacles from בור, this is still just בור.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, maybe the case is where he did not declare them ownerless? But according to שמואל, who says: we learned all of them from בור, that is still בור!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries a third reading: the objects landed but the owner never gave up ownership. It rejects this too, at least according to שמואל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The change is the ownership detail: now the owner still owns the objects. But שמואל holds that all obstacles in the street are learned from בור whether or not they were made הפקר. So for him, this case is still covered by בור and הצד השוה adds nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: He did not declare them ownerless
We learned all of them from his pit

phrases.english: Rather, where he did not declare them ownerless?
According to Shmuel, who says:
we learned all of them from his pit,
phrases.notes: "All of them" means all obstacles left in the street, even ones the owner did not give up.

phrases.english: that is the same as Pit!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Since the ownerless version was just בור, the גמרא tries the version where the owner kept them, and attacks that too.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading of אביי's case as landed objects that were not made הפקר.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: According to שמואל, even obstacles not made הפקר are learned from בור, so this case is still covered without הצד השוה.

steps.title: The objects are not like בור because the wind was involved
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the case really is where the owner made them הפקר, but they are not like בור. A בור does damage with no outside force, while these objects got there through the wind.
steps.simpleTranslation: Really, the case is where he declared them ownerless, and they are not like בור. What is special about בור is that no other force is mixed into it. Can you say the same about these, where another force is mixed into them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives its answer: go back to the ownerless case, but realize it cannot be learned from בור alone. So the משנה needs הצד השוה to include it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 7 showed that landed objects look exactly like בור. Now the גמרא finds one difference: a בור does damage with no outside force, but the wind brought these objects to where they lie. Because of this difference, בור alone cannot teach the case, and steps 10–12 show how the משנה's הצד השוה covers it.

keyTerms.meaning: Really / actually (going back to an earlier option)
They are not similar
Another force is mixed into it
Can you say? (asking if a rule really carries over)

steps.whatToRemember: אביי's roof case is objects blown down by the wind that did damage after landing and were made הפקר. They are like בור, but the wind was involved, so בור alone cannot teach them. That is why the משנה needs הצד השוה.
steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not saying these objects have nothing to do with בור. It is saying they have one extra feature (the wind) that בור lacks, so we cannot learn them from בור by itself.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows how הצד השוה works: it covers cases that mix features of different categories and so cannot be learned from any single one.

phrases.english: Really, where he declared them ownerless;
and they are not like Pit,
what is special about Pit –

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁכֵּן אֵין כֹּחַ אַחֵר מְעוֹרָב בּוֹ;
phrases.english: that no other force is mixed into it;
can you say the same about these,
where another force is mixed into them?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenges of steps 6 to 8 by returning to the ownerless case and showing why בור cannot teach it.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction: the case differs from the main category by an extra feature.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Landed objects that were made הפקר are simply בור, so הצד השוה is not needed.
steps.terutzMaskana: בור has no outside force involved, but these objects were moved by the wind, so they need הצד השוה to be included.

steps.title: Fire proves an outside force does not cancel liability
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers the problem from step 9 by pointing to אש, where an outside force helps and the owner is still liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: אש will prove it!
steps.whatsHappening: In step 9 the גמרא said these objects are not like בור because the wind brought them there. Now it answers: look at אש. The wind moves fire too, and the owner still pays.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The point raised against learning from בור was the 'outside force' of the wind. אש shows that an outside force does not free an owner from paying, because fire spreads with the wind and the owner is still liable. So that point cannot block the law.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Will prove.' The גמרא brings a case that shows a certain feature does not change the law.
Fire, one of the main categories of damage. An outside force (wind) helps it do damage.

steps.confusionAlert: 'אש תוכיח' does not mean we learn this case from אש alone. It only shows that the 'outside force' point raised against בור does not matter.

phrases.english: Fire will prove it!
phrases.notes: Fire also moves by an outside force, the wind, and its owner still pays. So the wind is no reason to be exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the problem raised in step 9 (the wind is an outside force) by bringing אש as a counter-example.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Because the wind moved the objects, they cannot be learned from בור, so maybe the owner is exempt.
steps.terutzMaskana: אש shows an outside force does not exempt the owner, so that difference does not matter.

steps.title: But fire naturally travels and does damage
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the proof from אש: fire's nature is to spread and damage, and these objects are not like that.
steps.simpleTranslation: What about אש? It is special, because its normal way is to move along and do damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back against step 10. It points out a special feature of אש that the wind-blown objects do not have.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אש naturally moves from place to place and causes damage. Objects sitting in the street do not travel and damage like that. So maybe the owner is liable for אש only because of this special feature, and we cannot learn the objects from it.

keyTerms.meaning: 'What about...?' A standard way to say: that source has a special feature, so you cannot learn from it.
Its normal way is to move along and do damage.

phrases.english: What about fire?
It is special, because its normal way is to move along and do damage.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the proof from אש brought in step 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: The proof from אש in step 10
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: אש has a special feature (it travels and damages) that the objects lack, so it cannot serve as the source for their law.

steps.title: בור proves that too, so we learn from both together
steps.stepSummary: בור shows that traveling to do damage is not needed for liability. So the law is learned from the shared features of בור and אש.
steps.simpleTranslation: בור will prove it! And the reasoning has come back around.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers step 11 by pointing to בור, which does not travel at all and is still liable. Then it says the reasoning has come full circle, so we learn from what בור and אש have in common.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each source has a special feature, but the other source shows that feature does not matter. בור does not move, and אש is moved by an outside force. What both share is that each is your property to guard and can cause damage. The wind-blown objects share these features too, so the owner is liable. This is how the משנה's הַצַּד הַשָּׁוֶה works.

keyTerms.meaning: 'The reasoning has come back around.' Each source cancels the other's special feature, so we learn from both together.
The common features shared by two sources, used to teach the law for a new case.

steps.whatToRemember: No single source works alone. בור has no outside force, and אש naturally travels. But together, through their shared features (yours to guard, able to damage), they teach that the owner of the wind-blown objects is liable.

phrases.english: Pit will prove it!
phrases.notes: A pit never moves anywhere, yet its owner pays. So traveling to do damage isn't needed.

phrases.english: And the reasoning has come back around.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 11 and closes the circle, so the case is learned from בור and אש together.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Counter-example, leading to learning from the shared features of both sources
steps.terutzHavaAmina: אש cannot teach this case, because fire naturally travels and damages.
steps.terutzMaskana: בור shows traveling is not needed. Together בור and אש teach the case through their shared features.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The wind-blown objects are covered by the משנה's הַצַּד הַשָּׁוֶה, learned from בור and אש together.

steps.title: רבא: it includes a בור-obstacle kicked to a new spot
steps.stepSummary: רבא gives a different case that the משנה's 'common features' rule comes to include: an obstacle moved by the feet of people or animals.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: It comes to include a בור-obstacle that gets rolled along by the feet of people or the feet of animals.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא offers his own answer to what the משנה's words come to add. He gives a new case: an obstacle that people's or animals' feet kicked to a different place, where it then caused damage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An obstacle in the street counts as a kind of בור. But if feet moved it to a new place, an outside force was involved, so it is not a plain בור. רבא says the הַצַּד הַשָּׁוֶה rule comes to make the owner liable in this case.

keyTerms.meaning: 'To include.' What extra case the words come to add.
That rolls or gets moved along.
Pit, a main category of damage. Here it means an obstacle someone left in a public place.

steps.whatToRemember: There are two views of what the משנה's הַצַּד הַשָּׁוֶה adds. The view in the earlier steps: objects the wind blew down. רבא: an obstacle kicked to a new spot by people's or animals' feet.

phrases.english: Rava said:
It comes to include a pit that gets rolled along
phrases.notes: 'Pit' here means an obstacle, like a stone, left in a public place. It works like a pit.

phrases.english: by the feet of people and the feet of animals.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the earlier line of reasoning ends, רבא offers a different case that the משנה's wording comes to include.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The משנה's הַצַּד הַשָּׁוֶה makes the owner liable for an obstacle that people or animals kicked to a new place where it did damage.

steps.title: What exact case is רבא talking about?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the case is. If the owner made the objects הפקר, both רב and שמואל would call it בור, so no special rule is needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If he made them ownerless, then according to both רב and שמואל, this is just בור.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבא's case by asking which situation he means. It starts with the first possibility: the owner made the objects הפקר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An obstacle in the street that the owner made הפקר is already treated as בור by everyone. If so, the משנה would not need its 'common features' rule to teach that the owner is liable. That would make רבא's suggestion pointless.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? What are the exact circumstances?
He made them ownerless (הפקר)
That is the same as

phrases.english: What is the case?
phrases.notes: The גמרא is asking about רבא's case from the last step: an obstacle moved by people's or animals' feet.

phrases.english: If he made them ownerless,
both according to רב and according to שמואל,
phrases.notes: רב and שמואל argue earlier about obstacles in the street. Both agree that if the owner made them ownerless, they count as a בור.

phrases.english: this is בור.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבא's case by asking for the exact circumstances.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's claim that the 'common features' rule is needed for an obstacle moved by feet.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the obstacle was made הפקר, it is already בור according to everyone, so the rule teaches nothing new.

steps.title: Showing that these objects match בור
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains why such objects are just like בור. Both are set up in a way that can cause damage, and the owner must guard both.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is special about בור? It was made in a way that leads to damage, and you must guard it. These objects too were set up in a way that leads to damage, and you must guard them!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up its challenge by showing that the defining features of בור also fit these objects.
steps.deeperAnalysis: בור has two key features: it was made in a way that can lead to damage, and the owner is responsible to guard it. These objects have both features, so they should simply count as בור. The משנה would not need a separate 'common features' rule for them.

keyTerms.meaning: What is different? What is special about?
From the start, it is made in a way that can cause damage
Guarding it is your responsibility

phrases.english: What is special about בור?
That from the start it is made for damage,
phrases.notes: "For damage" means made in a way that can cause harm, not made in order to harm someone.

phrases.english: and guarding it is upon you.
These too:
from the start they are made for damage,
and guarding them is upon you!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains and strengthens the challenge from step 14.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that a הפקר obstacle needs a separate source beyond בור.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The features that define בור (made in a way that can damage, owner must guard it) are all present here, so it is simply בור.

steps.title: What if the owner did not make them ownerless?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tries the other possibility: the owner did not make them הפקר. But שמואל says all obstacles are learned from בור anyway, so it is still בור.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, is it where he did not make them ownerless? According to שמואל, who says all of them are learned from בור, this is still בור!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tests the second possibility, where the owner kept ownership. Even here, according to שמואל, it is still just בור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל holds that any obstacle left in the street is learned from בור, whether or not it was made הפקר. So even this second possibility does not need the 'common features' rule. Both options seem to fail, and the next step answers this.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather (used to try another possibility)
We learned all of them from his בור

phrases.english: Rather, where he did not make them ownerless?
According to שמואל, who says,
"We learned all of them from his pit,"
phrases.notes: "All of them" means all obstacles left in the street, even ones he never made ownerless.

phrases.english: this is בור!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries the opposite case after the first one failed.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's case, now read as a case where the objects were not made הפקר.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: According to שמואל, even obstacles that were not made הפקר are בור, so the rule is still not needed.

steps.title: It is הפקר, but not like בור, because feet moved it
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the case really is one where the owner made the objects הפקר. Still, they are not like בור: the owner's own actions made the בור, but here passersby moved the object.
steps.simpleTranslation: Really, it is where he made them ownerless, and it is not like בור. What is special about בור is that his own actions caused it. Can you say the same about these, where his actions did not cause it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers both challenges. It goes back to the הפקר case and shows why it still differs from בור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a בור, the owner's own digging creates the danger. Here, other people's feet kicked the object to the spot where it did damage. So בור alone cannot teach this case, and the משנה's 'common features' rule is needed after all.

keyTerms.meaning: Really, actually (going back to the first possibility)
What is special about... (shows a weakness in a comparison)
His own actions caused it
Can you say (the same)?

steps.whatToRemember: This copies the pattern from the wind case in steps 9–12, but with a different distinction. There, בור differed because no outside force is involved. Here, בור differs because the owner's own actions made it, while this obstacle was moved by passersby's feet. That is why the משנה's 'common features' rule is needed.
steps.whyThisMatters: This step makes clear what makes בור special: the owner's own action creates the danger. That is why cases moved by outside forces need a separate source.

phrases.english: Really, it is where he made them ownerless;
and it is not similar to בור:
what is special about בור?
That his actions caused it;
will you say the same about these,
where his actions did not cause it?
phrases.notes: Here people's or animals' feet moved the object to the place where it did the damage.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenges of steps 14–16.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction: the case is הפקר, but it differs from בור in how the damage came about.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A הפקר obstacle is just a בור, so the 'common features' rule is not needed.
steps.terutzMaskana: Since passersby's feet, not the owner, moved the object, בור alone cannot teach it, so the 'common features' rule is needed.

steps.title: שור shows that the owner's own action is not needed
steps.stepSummary: Against the objection that the owner did not personally create the obstacle, the גמרא points to שור. The owner does not make his ox do damage, and he is still liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let שור prove it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the problem from step 17. It brings שור as proof that the owner can be liable even when he did not cause the damage himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 17 said the obstacle is unlike בור, because בור was made by the owner and this obstacle was moved by passersby. The גמרא answers that with שור the owner also does nothing, yet he pays. So 'the owner did not do it' is not a reason to exempt him.

keyTerms.meaning: Will prove: a case that shows a feature does not matter
Ox: the main damage category of an owner's animal

phrases.english: Ox will prove it!
phrases.notes: Your ox damages without you doing anything, and you still pay. So that difference can't free you here.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 17's point that the obstacle differs from בור because the owner did not create it.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Counter-example from another main damage category
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since the owner did not move the obstacle himself, maybe he is exempt.
steps.terutzMaskana: With שור the owner also does not act, yet he is liable. So the owner's own action is not required.

steps.title: But שור moves around by nature
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back: שור is different because an ox naturally walks around and does damage. An obstacle does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: What about שור? It is special, since its way is to go about and cause damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the proof from שור. An ox is unlike a stone lying in the street.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An ox moves on its own and tends to cause damage. An obstacle sits still and does not wander. So we cannot learn the obstacle from שור alone.

keyTerms.meaning: 'What about...?': a formula that points to what makes the source case different
Its normal way is to move and cause damage

phrases.aramaic: מָה לְשׁוֹר, שֶׁכֵּן דַּרְכּוֹ לֵילֵךְ וּלְהַזִּיק.
phrases.english: What about an ox? Its way is to go and cause damage.

steps.triggerLanguage: מָה לְשׁוֹר, שֶׁכֵּן דַּרְכּוֹ לֵילֵךְ וּלְהַזִּיק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the proof from שור given in step 18.
steps.kashyaTarget: Learning the obstacle's law from שור
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: שור has a feature the obstacle lacks: it naturally moves and does damage. So it cannot be the source.

steps.title: בור shows that moving around is not needed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers with בור. A pit does not move around at all, yet its owner is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let בור prove it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers step 19 by pointing back to בור. A pit stays still and the owner still pays.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 19 said the obstacle is unlike שור because it does not move by itself. But a בור also does not move, and its owner is liable. So 'it doesn't wander and damage' is no reason to exempt him either.

keyTerms.meaning: Pit: the main damage category of a hazard left in place

phrases.english: Pit will prove it!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 19's objection to the proof from שור.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Counter-example from another main damage category
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since the obstacle does not naturally move and damage, maybe the owner is exempt.
steps.terutzMaskana: בור also does not move, yet its owner is liable. So that feature is not required.

steps.title: The proof circles back to what בור and שור share
steps.stepSummary: Each category answers the weakness of the other. So the law comes from what שור and בור have in common: the הצד השוה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the reasoning has come back around: this one's special feature is not like that one's special feature.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא ends the back-and-forth. Neither בור nor שור alone is the source, so we learn from what they share.
steps.deeperAnalysis: בור's special feature (the owner made it) is not needed, as שור shows. שור's special feature (it moves around) is not needed, as בור shows. What they share is that both can damage and the owner must guard them. The obstacle moved by passersby has that too, so it is included. This finishes defending רבא's case from step 13.

keyTerms.meaning: The reasoning has come back around: a formula that ends this kind of proof
The feature of this one is not like the feature of that one
The common feature shared by two sources

steps.whatToRemember: When each source has a special feature that the other source shows is not needed, the law is learned from the feature they share (הצד השוה). That is how רבא's obstacle moved by passersby is included.

phrases.english: And the reasoning has come back around:
the feature of this one is not like the feature of that one.
phrases.notes: Literally, 'the seeing of this is not like the seeing of that.' Each has its own trait, so we learn from what they share.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְחָזַר הַדִּין, לֹא רְאִי זֶה כִרְאִי זֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Sums up the back-and-forth of steps 18–20 and closes רבא's approach.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רבא's case (an obstacle moved by people or animals) is learned from the common feature of שור and בור.

steps.title: Another case included: gutters and caves emptied into the street
steps.stepSummary: רב אדא בר אהבה says the משנה's rule comes to include a case from a ברייתא. People may empty gutters and caves into the street in the rainy season, but if this causes damage, they must pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אדא בר אהבה said: The rule comes to include what was taught in a ברייתא. All those the חכמים spoke of, who open their gutters and clear out their caves: in the summer they have no permission, and in the rainy season they have permission. Even though they act with permission, if they cause damage, they must pay.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אדא בר אהבה gives a different answer to the question of what the משנה's 'common features' rule comes to add. His case is people who drain dirty water into the street.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the rainy season the חכמים allow people to empty gutters and caves into the public street. Even so, the ברייתא says they pay for any damage this causes. The new point is that having permission does not cancel liability. רב אדא בר אהבה says this is the case the משנה's rule comes to include.

keyTerms.meaning: To include: to bring in a case that would otherwise be left out
Open their gutters or drains into the street
Clear out (flush) their caves or cellars
Permission
The rainy season

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think that having permission means you are free from paying. The ברייתא says clearly that even with permission, you pay for damage.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a key idea in the laws of damages: being allowed to do something does not exempt you from paying for the harm it causes.

phrases.english: Rav Adda bar Ahava said:
It comes to include that which was taught in a ברייתא:
All those about whom they said
that they may open their gutters
and clear out their caves:
in the summer, they do not have permission;
in the rainy season, they have permission.
Even though it is with permission,
if they caused damage, they are obligated to pay.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אַדָּא בַּר אַהֲבָה אָמַר, לְאֵתוֹיֵי הָא דְּתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different case from רבא's for what the משנה's common-features rule comes to include.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: People allowed to empty gutters and caves into the street in the rainy season must still pay for damage. רב אדא בר אהבה says the משנה's rule comes to include this case.

steps.title: When does the poured-out waste do damage?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the case is, and rules out damage done while the waste is still flowing, since that is the person's own force.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If the waste does damage while it is still flowing, that is his own force!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what exact case רב אדא בר אהבה means. It throws out the first option right away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the waste hurts someone while it is still moving from his pouring, the person himself is doing the damage. That is plain damage by a person, and it needs no הצד השוה. So this cannot be the case the משנה's rule comes to include.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? What are the exact circumstances?
While they are moving or flowing
His force. Damage done by the push of the person himself.

phrases.english: What are the circumstances?
If they cause damage while they are flowing,
phrases.notes: "They" means the water and waste poured out of the gutters and caves in step 22.

phrases.english: it is his own force!

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵיכִי דָּמֵי? אִי בַּהֲדֵי דְּקָאָזְלִי מַזְּקִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the case brought in step 22 to see if it really needs the הצד השוה.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב אדא בר אהבה's claim that the משנה's rule includes the gutters case
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the damage happens while the waste is flowing, it is the person's own force. That is already covered as damage by a person, so the הצד השוה would add nothing.

steps.title: The case is after the waste settles
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the case is damage done after the waste has come to rest.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is after it has come to rest.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the case is after the waste has stopped flowing and is lying in the street.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the waste is lying still, it is no longer the person's push. It is now an obstacle in the street. This sets up the next question: what kind of damage is such an obstacle?

keyTerms.meaning: After
It came to rest, it settled

phrases.english: Rather, it is after it has come to rest.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 23 by moving the case to after the waste settles.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The damage might happen while the waste is flowing.
steps.terutzMaskana: The damage happens after the waste is lying still.

steps.title: If he declared it ownerless, it is just בור
steps.stepSummary: If the owner declared the waste ownerless, both רב and שמואל would call it בור. It matches בור's features exactly, so there is no need for a הצד השוה.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If he declared them ownerless, then according to both רב and שמואל this is בור. What is special about בור? It is made from the start in a way that can cause damage, it is your property, and guarding it is your job. These too are made from the start in a way that can cause damage, they are your property, and guarding them is your job!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks whether the owner declared the waste ownerless. If he did, the waste is simply a kind of בור, so the הצד השוה is still not needed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא lists what defines בור: it is made in a way that can cause damage, and guarding it is your job. The settled waste has the same features. So it fits under בור directly, and the question of what the הצד השוה adds comes back.

keyTerms.meaning: He declared them ownerless (הֶפְקֵר)
What is different? What is special about it?
It is made from the start in a way that can cause damage
Guarding it is your responsibility

phrases.english: What are the circumstances?
If he declared them ownerless,

phrases.aramaic: בֵּין לְרַב בֵּין לִשְׁמוּאֵל הַיְינוּ בּוֹר;
phrases.english: both according to Rav and according to Shmuel, this is Pit;
what is special about Pit?
That from the start it is made in a way that can cause damage,
and it is your property, and guarding it is upon you;
these too: from the start they are made in a way that can cause damage,
and they are your property, and guarding them is upon you!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer of step 24 by splitting the settled-waste case into two options. This step handles the first option.
steps.kashyaTarget: The settled-waste case as something the הצד השוה must include
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Ownerless settled waste has every feature of בור. So it is learned straight from בור, and the הצד השוה adds nothing.
steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not asking whether the owner is liable. It agrees he is. It is asking which source makes him liable, and whether that source has to be the הצד השוה.

steps.title: Maybe he did not declare it ownerless
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests a second option: the case is where the owner did not declare the waste ownerless.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is where he did not declare them ownerless?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries the other option: the owner kept the waste as his own. This sets up the next challenge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the owner never gave up ownership, maybe the waste is not a typical בור. Then the הצד השוה would be needed to make him liable. The next step tests this suggestion.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather. It brings in a new suggestion.
Where he did not declare them ownerless
The common feature, the shared point of two categories

phrases.english: Rather, it is where he did not declare them ownerless?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 25 by switching to the other option.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The case was ownerless waste, which is simply בור.
steps.terutzMaskana: Perhaps the case is waste that still belongs to him.

steps.title: For שמואל, it is still בור
steps.stepSummary: שמואל holds that all obstacles are learned from בור, even if not declared ownerless. So for him this case is still בור.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to שמואל, who says, "We learned all of them from his pit," this is בור!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the new suggestion according to שמואל. In his view, even an obstacle that was not declared ownerless counts as בור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל learns liability for every obstacle from בור, whether or not the owner gave up ownership. So for him, the second option also fits under בור. The הצד השוה would still add nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: We learned all of them from his pit. Every obstacle is learned from בור.
This is the same as

phrases.english: According to Shmuel, who says:
We learned all of them from his pit,
phrases.notes: "All of them" means every obstacle left in the street, even if it was not declared ownerless.

phrases.english: this is Pit!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Knocks down the suggestion of step 26, at least according to שמואל.
steps.kashyaTarget: The suggestion that the case is waste that was not declared ownerless
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: שמואל learns all obstacles from בור, even ones not declared ownerless. So the case is still בור, and the הצד השוה is not needed.

steps.title: Ownerless, but poured with permission
steps.stepSummary: The case really is ownerless waste. It is still different from בור, because a בור is dug without permission, while this waste was poured out with permission.
steps.simpleTranslation: Really, it is where he declared them ownerless. But it is not like בור. What is special about בור is that it is made without permission. Would you say the same about these, which are done with permission?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the first option, ownerless waste. It shows why בור alone cannot teach this case, so the הצד השוה is needed after all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Digging a pit in the street is done without permission. Pouring out gutters in the rainy season is allowed. Someone could argue that an allowed act should not bring liability. So בור alone is not enough to teach this case. That is why the משנה's הצד השוה is needed to include it.

keyTerms.meaning: Really, in truth. It goes back to an earlier option.
And it is not similar
What about this one, which has this special feature? A way of showing a source is not strong enough.
With permission / without permission

steps.whatToRemember: The gutters case is ownerless waste lying in the street. It cannot be learned from בור alone, because a בור is dug without permission and this waste was poured out with permission. So the משנה's הצד השוה is what makes the owner liable.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that the הצד השוה really adds something. It makes a person liable even for damage caused by something he was allowed to do.

phrases.english: Actually, it is where he declared them ownerless;
and it is not similar to Pit:
what about Pit? It is special in that it is made without permission,
will you say the same about these, which are done with permission?
phrases.notes: The ברייתא in step 22 allows emptying gutters into the street in the rainy season. That's the permission here.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenges of steps 25 and 27 by returning to the ownerless case and showing a real difference from בור.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Showing a difference between the case and its supposed source
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Ownerless waste is exactly like בור, so the הצד השוה is not needed.
steps.terutzMaskana: A בור is made without permission, but this waste was poured out with permission. So בור alone cannot teach it, and the הצד השוה is needed.
